A vast red-rock plain freckled with the first spreading patches of green moss and lichen, the living color pooling in the low ground while the high ridges stay barren and rust-colored.
A half-transformed world seen wide — green spreading in a great tide outward from a cluster of domes, fading into the old red desert at its edges where the two worlds meet.
Newly filled oceans steam under a young sun, pale mist rising off the fresh seas, raw coastlines of red rock just beginning to green at the waterline where wet meets stone.
A sharp atmospheric front cuts the sky in two — one half bruised and alive with storm-clouds seeding new rain, the other half the old clear rust-colored void above dead desert.
Lichen pushes slowly over bare basalt slabs, a slow orange and grey creep across the rock face, the stone beneath it unchanged for a billion years and the life above it days old.
Young forests of thin pale trees stand under a hazy thickening sky, the canopy barely waist-high, surrounded on all sides by the flat red emptiness that still owns most of the world.
A river has found its first channel, cutting a dark wet groove across the ancient dust, the banks just beginning to fuzz with the faint green of new grass and waterside moss.
A valley floor gone entirely green while the ridgelines above it remain hard and red, the living carpet filling the low bowl like water settling, stopped exactly where the elevation rises.
Tundra grasses are pushing through the gravel flats, thin and wind-flattened, giving the brown plain a faint living tint — not yet grass, not yet desert, caught halfway between the two.
A coastline where a new sea laps at red sand, the waterline stained dark with moisture, a thin fringe of green algae just beginning to colonize the rocks at the tide's reach.
The first rain falls on stone that has never known rain, each drop cratering dry dust, tiny rivulets running rust-red through channels they are carving for the very first time under grey clouds.

Dome clusters sit behind glass while just outside, the first unprotected seedling meadow struggles in the open air, green inside the perimeter fence, pure red rock stretching away beyond it in all directions.

A frozen highland plateau cracks under new warmth, ice that formed under a different sky melting into shallow ponds that reflect clouds above — the shorelines already ringed with the first algal growth.
A canyon system carved by ancient dry winds now holds a thin ribbon of river at its base, the walls still raw red stone, the water threading through them impossibly silver and new.
Grasslands roll across the lowland basin but stop at the foot of the volcanic escarpment rising above, the rock face above the grass line bare and orange, the contrast a clean horizontal seam.

The terminator zone at dusk shows the difference clearly — sunlit slopes deep green with new growth, shadowed slopes still bare red, the line of light dividing two different centuries of the same world.
An ancient crater filled now with a shallow lake, the water clear and cold, ringed by reed-like plants at the margins while the outer crater walls above stay raw and uncolonized basalt.
Spore clouds drift on the new wind from a seeding aircraft, settling over bare red rock in a faint green haze, the land below the flight path already beginning to blur with new color.

A mountain's lower slopes gone green with creeping groundcover, but the peak above the snow line still bare and iron-red, the living zone advancing upward measurably every season, not yet at the summit.
Wetlands are forming where water has pooled in the flats, dark reedy growth spreading outward from the wet center, the surrounding plain still powder-dry and brick-red beyond the moisture's reach.

Jellyfish-pale fungi push up through cracked ground near the dome exhaust vents, improbable white shapes on an orange plain, the first decomposers arriving before there is yet anything dead to decompose.
A dust storm passes over a greening basin, the red cloud rolling across new grass, depositing the old dead world like a thin layer of memory over the living surface below it.
A wide aerial view shows the terraformed zone as an island, green oval in an infinite red sea, the border between them soft and ragged, the green losing ground at its northern edge.
Thick moss carpets the floor of a lava tube whose ceiling has collapsed, the sheltered microclimate hosting dense life while ten meters away through the broken wall the open plain is still bare rock.

A hilltop at the green zone's frontier — behind, a living meadow with insects and wind-bent grass; ahead, pure red desert to the horizon with not one living thing, the exact edge of what has been done.
